rationale: A wins because it separates four real stories cleanly: markets math, regulated-enterprise buying, self-reported benchmarks, and open-model business economics. Its line "Databricks graded its own model, and that is the part enterprises should check" is the uncomfortable story in the room and it names the proof burden before the founder embarrasses themselves. B has useful instincts, but "Databricks claims $3B ARR and 60% growth — unaudited, on its own benchmarks, before any public filing" jams revenue provenance and model benchmarks into one bucket, then overstates "unaudited" beyond the update. That is not fatal, but it is sloppy enough to lose.
gaps_in_A: The fourth angle is a touch more analytical than newsy: "No urgent hook" is honest, but it means this is weaker than the first three unless an exec or analyst gives it muscle.

"banks, hospitals, and insurers" are plausible examples of regulated buyers, but only "regulated enterprises" is in the update; A handles this mostly as beat framing, not fact, but it should keep examples clearly hypothetical.

It could more explicitly warn that "open license" does not necessarily mean open source; it asks the right question later, but the headline says "gives away for free," which may outrun the license economics.
gaps_in_B: Invents or overstates legal/procurement detail: "regulated enterprises cannot send proprietary data to third-party inference APIs" is not in the update and is too categorical.
Overclaims verification status with "unaudited" and "before any public filing." The update says the benchmarks are company-owned and Databricks is private; it does not say revenue is unaudited.

Padded overlap: the second angle's business-model thesis and the third angle's financial-credibility thesis both orbit the same $3B/60% proof problem, while A separates revenue, benchmark accountability, and monetization more cleanly.

"Banks and hospitals want AI models they can audit" is a strong headline, but auditability is not supplied as a fact. The update says open license and fine-tuning on own data, not audit logging or audit rights.
